opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there are a few different ways it helps, and some of them are pretty direct while others are more subtle.

The most direct one is just that we use it ourselves, constantly. A huge fraction of the code written at Anthropic now goes through Claude Code in some form, and that includes the code for training infrastructure, evals, research experiments, all of it. So when the model gets better, our researchers get faster, and that speeds up the next model. There's a real compounding loop there, and you feel it day to day. Somebody who used to spend a week wiring up an experiment can now spend an afternoon on it and spend the rest of the week actually thinking about the results.

The second piece is that Claude Code is one of the best windows we have into where the model actually falls short. Chat is great, but agentic coding is a much harder test. The model has to plan, use tools, recover from its own mistakes, keep track of context over a long task, and know when to stop and ask a human. When it fails at those things, it fails in really legible ways: the tests don't pass, it went down a rabbit hole, it edited the wrong file. That gives us very concrete signal about what to work on, whether that's long-horizon reliability, instruction following, or calibration about its own uncertainty.

Third, and this matters a lot to me from a safety perspective, it's a place where we can learn how agents should behave when they have real power in someone's environment. Things like: when should it confirm before running a destructive command? How does it handle a prompt injection sitting in some file it read? How do you keep it honest about whether the tests actually passed? Those questions are going to matter much more as models get more capable and more autonomous, and coding is a relatively contained domain where we can work them out now with real users rather than just in theory.

And then I'd say the last thing is it shapes our intuitions about what "helpful" means. Developers are very demanding users. They'll tell you immediately if the model is being lazy, overconfident, or annoying. That feedback ends up informing how we think about the model's character and judgment more broadly, not just its coding ability.

So it's not just a product. It's kind of a flywheel for the research itself.

r001.rationale: The response says Anthropic researchers use Claude Code constantly, see legible failures firsthand, and get concrete signals about what to work on, connecting that experience to addressing weaknesses.

r002.rationale: It calls Claude Code a window into where the model falls short and says agentic coding reveals specific limitations such as reliability, instruction following, and uncertainty calibration.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think Claude Code is one of the most important things we've built, and not just as a product. The way I think about it is that it closes a loop that used to be really slow for us.

Historically, the way you'd improve a model at coding was you'd train it, you'd run it against some benchmarks, maybe you'd hand it to a few internal users, and then weeks later you'd get some vague signal about what was working and what wasn't. With Claude Code, the model is out there doing real work in real repos, with real engineers who are impatient and have high standards. That's a very different kind of signal. You find out very quickly where the model gets confused, where it over-engineers things, where it gives up too early, where it's too confident about something it hasn't actually verified.

And a lot of that shows up internally first, because our own engineers use it constantly. I'd say the majority of the code at Anthropic now involves Claude in some way. So when the model has a bad habit, we feel it ourselves, and that creates a lot of pressure to fix it. It's dogfooding in the most literal sense. Our researchers are using the thing to build the next version of the thing.

The other piece is that Claude Code is an agent, and agentic behavior is really hard to evaluate in the abstract. Can the model plan? Can it recover when a test fails? Does it know when to stop and ask instead of charging ahead? Does it actually run the code before saying it's done? Those are the capabilities we care most about for the next generation of models, and the only way to really understand them is to watch the model operate over long horizons with real tools and real consequences. Claude Code gives us that environment. It tells us what "good" looks like in a way a static benchmark just can't.

And then honestly, there's a safety angle too. If we're going to have models that take hundreds of actions on your behalf, we need to understand how they behave when they're given that kind of autonomy. Coding is a relatively contained domain to learn those lessons in. The feedback is fast, the mistakes are usually recoverable, and you learn a lot about how to make an agent that's both capable and trustworthy. That knowledge feeds straight back into how we train and evaluate everything else.

So it's a product, but it's also a research instrument. It's how we find out what the model actually is, as opposed to what we think it is.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Anthropic engineers use Claude Code constantly, feel the model’s bad habits themselves, and that this creates pressure to fix them.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes Claude Code revealing where the model gets confused, over-engineers, gives up, or acts too confidently, and says it helps researchers learn what the model actually is.

astra-6.text:
I think Claude Code gives us a really useful feedback loop. When you’re working in a codebase, the model has to do more than produce an answer that sounds right. It has to understand the context, make a change, run tests, and respond when something breaks. That gives us concrete signals about where it’s succeeding and where it still needs work.

And using it ourselves helps us understand which improvements actually matter. Can it stay on task longer? Can it recognize when it needs more information? Can it recover from a mistake? Those are coding capabilities, but they’re also capabilities you want in a broadly useful AI assistant.

r001.rationale: The response says using Claude Code helps identify where the model needs work and which improvements matter, but does not state that personally experiencing its weaknesses motivates researchers to fix them.

r002.rationale: The response says using Claude Code provides concrete signals about where the model still needs work and helps researchers understand which improvements matter, communicating a better understanding of its limitations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Claude Code gives us a really tight feedback loop. We use it internally, so we get to see where the model is useful and where it gets stuck on real work. Can it navigate a codebase, make a change, run the tests, and recover when something goes wrong? Those are much richer signals than whether it can answer a coding question in isolation.

And then there’s this compounding effect: as the models get better, Claude Code becomes more useful to the people building the next models. It can help with experiments, debugging, and the engineering around research. That doesn’t mean the whole process suddenly becomes autonomous, but it can make our researchers and engineers more productive, which helps us improve the models faster.

r001.rationale: The response says internal use reveals where the model gets stuck, but does not say that experiencing those weaknesses motivates researchers to fix them.

r002.rationale: The response says internal use lets them see where the model is useful and where it gets stuck on real work, communicating a better understanding of its limitations.
